statements.text: If A is an event of S, i.e. A ⊂ S, then P(A) = n(A)/n(S). Formula: $P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(S)}$
n(A) is the number of elements of the event A, n(S) is the number of elements of sample space S, and P(A) is the probability of occurring event A.
Note that: It is said that an event occurred if the outcome of the experiment is an element of the elements of the set expressing this event.

statements.text: If A and B are two events from a sample space (S), then the intersection of the two events A and B, denoted by the symbol A ∩ B, means the events A and B occur together. Formula: $A \cap B$
The two events B and C cannot occur at the same time so we say B and C are mutually exclusive events.
A and B are mutually exclusive events if $A\cap B=\phi$.
A set of events is mutually exclusive if every pair of them is mutually exclusive.
Remark: if A and B are mutually exclusive events from sample space S (as in the figure), then the following hold.
For mutually exclusive events, A ∩ B is the empty set. Formula: $A \cap B = \phi$
P(A ∩ B) = (number of elements of φ)/(number of elements of S) = Zero/(number of elements of S) = Zero. Formula: $P(A \cap B)=\frac{n(\phi)}{n(S)}=\frac{0}{n(S)}=0$

context.text: Imagine 10 students on a school trip, numbered 1 to 10, and the teacher picks one number at random. Suppose students 1 to 6 brought sandwiches (event $A$), students 4 to 7 brought juice (event $B$), and students 9 and 10 brought nothing (event $C$). Which students are in both $A$ and $B$, that is $A \cap B$, and what is the probability that the chosen student brought sandwiches and juice? Then decide whether $A$ and $C$ can happen at the same time.

statements.text: If A and B are two events from the sample space S, the union of the two events, denoted $A\cup B$, means the occurrence of the two events A or B or both, i.e. occurrence of at least one event.
If A and B are two mutually exclusive events then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Formula: $P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$

context.text: Imagine a school raffle with 10 tickets numbered 1 to 10 in a box, and one ticket is drawn at random. You win a prize if the ticket is an even number (event $A$) or a multiple of 5 (event $B$), or both. What is the probability of winning, $P(A \cup B)$? Try to work it out using $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$, so the overlapping ticket is not counted twice.
